It lies towards the galactic bulge, where thick dust dims it significantly. Without this obscuration M9 would appear nearly a magnitude brighter and be visible to the naked eye.
dso/m9.fun_fact: M9 suffers more interstellar dust absorption than almost any other Messier globular — about 1.3 magnitudes of dimming compared to a clear line of sight. Two smaller globular clusters (NGC 6342 and NGC 6356) lie within about 1° of M9, making it the centre of a remarkable grouping of three globulars in a small patch of sky.

dso/m90.description: Messier 90 is a large spiral galaxy in Virgo, and the textbook example of an "anemic" galaxy.
dso/m90.fun_fact: M90 has had its star-forming gas stripped away by its plunge through the Virgo Cluster, leaving tails of glowing gas up to 260,000 light-years long!

dso/m91.description: Messier 91 is a barred spiral galaxy in Coma Berenices and the faintest object in the Messier catalogue.
dso/m91.fun_fact: M91 was lost for nearly 200 years! Messier recorded its position using the wrong reference galaxy, and it was only re-identified in 1969 by an amateur astronomer.

dso/m92.description: M92 is a bright globular cluster in Hercules, often overlooked because of its proximity to the more famous M13.
dso/m92.fun_fact: M92 is one of the oldest globular clusters at about 14.2 billion years old - nearly as old as the universe!

dso/m93.description: M93 is a bright, compact open cluster in Puppis, sitting in the rich southern Milky Way and easily found in binoculars. Its roughly 80 stars are arranged in a striking wedge or butterfly shape and include several hot blue supergiants, making it one of the more attractive open clusters in the winter sky.
dso/m93.fun_fact: M93 is relatively young — around 100 million years old — with dominant blue and blue-white stars that have not yet evolved into giants. It is one of the more southerly Messier clusters, and from latitudes north of about 50°N it never rises very high above the horizon.

dso/m94.description: M94 is a spiral galaxy in Canes Venatici with a bright inner ring where active star formation is occurring.
dso/m94.fun_fact: M94's inner ring is a starburst ring where new stars are forming at a very high rate!

dso/m95.description: Messier 95 is a barred spiral galaxy in Leo, part of the M96 Group along with M96 and M105.
dso/m95.fun_fact: A ring of furious star formation about 70,000 light-years wide circles M95's core, and a supernova flared there in 2012!

dso/m96.description: Messier 96 is a spiral galaxy in Leo, the brightest member of the M96 Group of galaxies.
dso/m96.fun_fact: M96 is roughly the same size and mass as our own Milky Way, but strikingly lopsided - its dust and gas are spread unevenly through its arms!

dso/m97.description: The Owl Nebula is a planetary nebula in Ursa Major, named for its owl-like appearance with two dark spots.
dso/m97.fun_fact: The dark owl eyes in M97 are three-dimensional cavities in the nebula, aligned with our line of sight!

dso/m98.description: Messier 98 is a spiral galaxy in Coma Berenices, seen nearly edge-on as part of the Virgo Cluster.
dso/m98.fun_fact: M98 is one of the rare galaxies moving toward us rather than away, closing at about 140 km/s!

dso/m99.description: Messier 99 is a grand design spiral galaxy in Coma Berenices, showing clear, sweeping spiral arms.
dso/m99.fun_fact: M99 was among the very first objects recognised as spiral, sketched by Lord Rosse in 1846 - and it forms stars three times faster than similar galaxies!

dso/n47_tucanae.description: 47 Tucanae (NGC 104) is the second-brightest globular cluster in the sky, a dense ball of roughly one million ancient stars orbiting the Milky Way in the constellation Tucana. At about 14,500 light-years away it appears to the naked eye as a fuzzy fourth-magnitude star, but a telescope resolves its compressed core into an extraordinary swarm of golden and blue-white suns. Its stars formed around 13 billion years ago, making the cluster almost as old as the universe itself.
dso/n47_tucanae.fun_fact: 47 Tucanae is a cosmic pulsar factory: astronomers have found at least 35 millisecond pulsars spinning hundreds of times per second inside it — more than in any other known globular cluster — the result of stellar close encounters that recycle old neutron stars by spinning them up.

dso/ngc_2903.description: NGC 2903 is a bright barred spiral galaxy in Leo, often called "the Messier object that Messier missed" — it is one of the most prominent galaxies in the sky not included in his famous catalogue. At magnitude 8.9 it is easily visible in binoculars and shows beautiful spiral structure in moderate telescopes.
dso/ngc_2903.fun_fact: NGC 2903 has one of the highest concentrations of star-forming "hotspots" known in a galaxy's central bar region — dense clusters of young massive stars lit up by intense star formation. It is used as a benchmark for studying starburst activity in barred spiral galaxies.

dso/ngc_6543.description: The Cat's Eye Nebula is one of the most structurally complex planetary nebulae known — a dying star's expelled gas sculpted into concentric shells, jets, and bright knots visible in Hubble imagery. In small telescopes it appears as a vivid blue-green disk in Draco, one of the most colourful objects in the autumn sky.
dso/ngc_6543.fun_fact: In 1864, astronomer William Huggins turned a spectroscope on the Cat's Eye and found it was made of glowing gas rather than unresolved stars — the first time the nature of any planetary nebula was confirmed. This discovery founded the field of nebular spectroscopy and overturned the prevailing view that all nebulae were distant star clusters.

dso/north_america_nebula.description: The North America Nebula (NGC 7000) is a large emission nebula in Cygnus whose shape remarkably resembles the continent of North America, complete with a Gulf of Mexico region. Spanning about 120 arcminutes across — roughly four times the diameter of the full Moon — it lies around 2,600 light-years away and is over 100 light-years wide.
dso/north_america_nebula.fun_fact: Despite its visual magnitude of 4, the nebula is too large and diffuse to see with the naked eye under most skies — yet it photographs beautifully, revealing the Cygnus Wall, a dense arc of intense star formation along its southern edge.

dso/omega_centauri.description: Omega Centauri is the largest and most massive globular cluster orbiting the Milky Way, containing roughly 10 million stars packed into a sphere about 150 light-years across. It is easily visible to the naked eye as a fuzzy star in Centaurus, and resolves into a breathtaking ball of stars through binoculars or any telescope.
dso/omega_centauri.fun_fact: Unlike typical globular clusters, Omega Centauri contains stars of many different ages and chemical compositions — a sign that it may be the stripped nucleus of a dwarf galaxy that was torn apart and swallowed by the Milky Way billions of years ago. It may even harbour a central intermediate-mass black hole.

dso/saturn_nebula.description: The Saturn Nebula is a planetary nebula in Aquarius named for its resemblance to the planet Saturn — extensions called ansae protrude from either side like ring handles, visible in moderate telescopes. At magnitude 8.0 it is one of the brightest planetary nebulae in the sky and shows complex structure in larger instruments.
dso/saturn_nebula.fun_fact: William Herschel discovered the Saturn Nebula in 1782 and noted its Saturn-like appearance. Modern observations reveal at least four distinct shells of gas surrounding the central white dwarf, reflecting multiple episodes of mass loss in the final stages of the star's life.

dso/sculptor_galaxy.description: The Sculptor Galaxy is one of the brightest and most beautiful edge-on spiral galaxies visible from Earth, appearing as an elongated glow in the southern constellation Sculptor. It is one of the closest starburst galaxies — a galaxy undergoing an intense burst of star formation — visible to amateur astronomers with binoculars from dark skies.
dso/sculptor_galaxy.fun_fact: The Sculptor Galaxy is one of the brightest members of the Sculptor Group — the galaxy group nearest to our own Local Group. Its central starburst region produces new stars at a rate several times higher than the Milky Way, driven by past interactions with neighbouring galaxies.

dso/sgr_a_star.description: Sagittarius A* (Sgr A*) is the supermassive black hole at the centre of the Milky Way, lying 26,000 light-years away in the direction of Sagittarius. With a mass of about 4 million solar masses compressed into a region smaller than our solar system, it is so dense that not even light can escape its event horizon.
dso/sgr_a_star.fun_fact: In 2022 the Event Horizon Telescope collaboration released the first direct image of Sgr A*, revealing a glowing ring of superheated gas surrounding its shadow — produced by combining data from radio observatories spread across the entire planet.

dso/smc.description: The Small Magellanic Cloud is a dwarf irregular satellite galaxy of the Milky Way, paired with its larger sibling the LMC. Together they are slowly being torn apart by the Milky Way's gravity, trailing a vast stream of gas across the sky.
dso/smc.fun_fact: By studying Cepheid variable stars in the SMC in 1908–12, Henrietta Swan Leavitt discovered the period-luminosity law — the breakthrough that first let astronomers measure distances across the universe!

dso/t_crb.description: T Coronae Borealis (T CrB) is a recurrent nova in Corona Borealis — a binary system of a red giant and a white dwarf. The white dwarf periodically accumulates enough hydrogen from its companion to trigger a thermonuclear explosion.
dso/t_crb.fun_fact: T CrB last erupted in 1946, briefly reaching magnitude 2.0 and becoming visible to the naked eye. Astronomers predict that another eruption is imminent — keep watching!

dso/tarantula_nebula.description: The Tarantula Nebula is the largest and most luminous star-forming region in the Local Group, a vast emission nebula embedded in the Large Magellanic Cloud spanning some 600 light-years. Despite lying 163,000 light-years away, it is bright enough to be visible to the naked eye.
dso/tarantula_nebula.fun_fact: If the Tarantula Nebula were as close as the Orion Nebula, it would be bright enough to cast shadows at night and would span half the visible sky!

dso/v838_mon.description: V838 Monocerotis is an unusual variable star in Monoceros that underwent a spectacular outburst in 2002, briefly becoming one of the most luminous stars in the Milky Way. Though far too faint for visual observers today, its expanding light echo — a wavefront of light illuminating ancient dust shells — produced some of the most dramatic Hubble Space Telescope images ever taken.
dso/v838_mon.fun_fact: The nature of V838 Mon's outburst remains debated. The leading theory is a stellar merger — two stars spiralling into each other and colliding — rather than a classic nova or supergiant eruption. If confirmed, it was the first real-time glimpse of a "luminous red nova," a rare class of explosion caused by stellar mergers, similar events have since been found in other galaxies.

dso/willman_1.description: Willman 1 is an ultra-faint dwarf satellite galaxy of the Milky Way, discovered in 2004 by Beth Willman in data from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey. It is one of the least luminous galaxies known and one of the most extreme laboratories for dark matter in the universe.
dso/willman_1.fun_fact: For every unit of ordinary matter in Willman 1, there are roughly 660 units of dark matter — making it amongst the most dark-matter-dominated objects ever discovered. Its stars also show signs of tidal disruption as the Milky Way slowly pulls it apart.

moon/europa.description: Europa is the second Galilean moon and is thought to harbour a vast liquid water ocean beneath its icy crust, making it one of the most promising places to search for life.
moon/europa.fun_fact: Europa's subsurface ocean may contain twice as much liquid water as all of Earth's oceans combined, kept liquid by tidal heating from Jupiter.

moon/io.description: Io is the innermost of Jupiter's four large Galilean moons and the most volcanically active body in the Solar System.
moon/io.fun_fact: Io has hundreds of active volcanoes, some erupting lava fountains dozens of kilometres high. Its constant activity is driven by tidal heating from Jupiter's enormous gravity.

moon/phobos.description: Phobos is the larger and innermost of Mars's two moons, orbiting closer to its planet than any other moon in the solar system. It is an irregularly shaped, heavily grooved and cratered body thought to be a captured asteroid.
moon/phobos.fun_fact: Phobos orbits Mars so quickly it rises in the west and sets in the east — and it is slowly spiralling inward, destined to either crash into Mars or break apart into a ring in about 50 million years.

planet/jupiter.description: Jupiter is the largest planet in our solar system. It's a gas giant with a famous Great Red Spot storm.
planet/jupiter.fun_fact: Jupiter has at least 95 known moons! Its largest moon, Ganymede, is bigger than the planet Mercury.

planet/mars.description: Mars is the fourth planet from the Sun, known as the Red Planet due to iron oxide on its surface.
planet/mars.fun_fact: Mars has the largest volcano in the solar system: Olympus Mons, which is about 2.5 times taller than Mount Everest!

planet/mercury.description: Mercury is the smallest planet and closest to the Sun. A year on Mercury lasts only 88 Earth days.
planet/mercury.fun_fact: Despite being closest to the Sun, Mercury is not the hottest planet. Venus is hotter due to its thick atmosphere!

planet/moon.description: The Moon is Earth's only natural satellite. It influences our tides and has been visited by 12 astronauts.
planet/moon.fun_fact: The Moon is slowly drifting away from Earth at about 3.8 cm per year. It was much closer billions of years ago!

planet/neptune.description: Neptune is the most distant planet in our Solar System. It has the strongest winds, reaching 2,100 km/h.
planet/neptune.fun_fact: Neptune was discovered through mathematics! Scientists predicted its location before anyone saw it through a telescope.

planet/pluto.description: Pluto is a dwarf planet in the Kuiper Belt. It was considered the ninth planet until 2006.
planet/pluto.fun_fact: Pluto has a heart-shaped glacier made of nitrogen ice, visible in images from NASA's New Horizons mission!

planet/saturn.description: Saturn is the sixth planet from the Sun, famous for its spectacular ring system made of ice and rock.
planet/saturn.fun_fact: Saturn is so light it would float in water! Its density is less than water, though there's no bathtub big enough to test this.

planet/sun.description: The Sun is the star at the centre of our solar system. It provides the light and heat that makes life on Earth possible.
planet/sun.fun_fact: The Sun contains 99.86% of all the mass in our solar system. About 1.3 million Earths could fit inside it!

planet/uranus.description: Uranus is an ice giant that rotates on its side. It was the first planet discovered using a telescope.
planet/uranus.fun_fact: Uranus rotates on its side at a 98-degree tilt, possibly due to a collision with an Earth-sized object long ago!

planet/venus.description: Venus is the second planet from the Sun and the hottest in our solar system. It's often called Earth's twin due to similar size.
planet/venus.fun_fact: A day on Venus is longer than its year! It takes 243 Earth days to rotate once, but only 225 days to orbit the Sun.

shower/aquariids.description: The Eta Aquariids are one of two annual showers produced by debris from Halley's Comet. Peaking at up to 70 meteors per hour, the shower strongly favours the southern hemisphere, where the radiant rises high before dawn. Northern observers still enjoy a respectable rate of 30 or more per hour.
shower/aquariids.fun_fact: Eta Aquariid meteors travel at 66 km/s — fast enough that the ionised air they create can glow for several seconds after the meteor has gone. You may see Halley's ancient dust burning up in front of your eyes, shed during one of the comet's many visits thousands of years ago.

shower/deltaaquariids.description: The Southern Delta Aquariids peak in late July and are best seen from tropical and southern latitudes, where the radiant in Aquarius climbs high before dawn. They produce a steady stream of medium-speed meteors at up to 16 per hour, with few bright fireballs.
shower/deltaaquariids.fun_fact: The exact parent body of the Delta Aquariids remains uncertain. The leading candidate is Comet 96P/Machholz, an unusual short-period comet with a highly tilted orbit that swings remarkably close to the Sun — closer than the planet Mercury.

shower/geminids.description: The Geminids are widely regarded as the finest meteor shower of the year — prolific (up to 120 per hour), reliable, and active from early evening rather than only after midnight. They radiate from the constellation Gemini and produce a wide range of meteor brightnesses, including vivid fireballs.
shower/geminids.fun_fact: Uniquely among major showers, the Geminids come from an asteroid rather than a comet: 3200 Phaethon, a "rock comet" whose orbit takes it closer to the Sun than any other named asteroid. The extreme heat may fracture its rocky surface and drive off the dust that produces the shower.

shower/leonids.description: The Leonids radiate from the sickle of Leo and typically produce around 20 meteors per hour. They are famous for spectacular storms that erupt roughly every 33 years when Earth passes through a dense dust filament shed by Comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle. These storms can produce thousands of meteors per hour.
shower/leonids.fun_fact: The 1833 Leonid storm produced an estimated 100,000 meteors per hour, terrifying observers across North America who feared the sky was on fire. The event launched the scientific study of meteor showers. Comparable storms occurred in 1966 and 1999.

shower/lyrids.description: The Lyrids are a reliable spring shower radiating from near the bright star Vega in Lyra. They produce swift, moderately bright meteors, peaking at around 18 per hour, and occasionally generate fireballs that leave glowing smoke trails.
shower/lyrids.fun_fact: The Lyrids are the oldest reliably recorded meteor shower in history. Chinese astronomers documented a storm of meteors "falling like rain" in 687 BCE. The debris comes from Comet Thatcher, which takes 415 years to orbit the Sun and last visited the inner solar system in 1861.

shower/orionids.description: The Orionids are the second meteor shower produced each year by Halley's Comet, radiating from near the raised club of Orion. Peaking at around 25 per hour, they are known for fast, often bright meteors that frequently leave glowing ionisation trains lasting several seconds.
shower/orionids.fun_fact: Halley's Comet is responsible for two annual meteor showers: the Eta Aquariids in May, when Earth crosses the comet's outbound debris trail, and the Orionids in October, when Earth crosses the inbound trail. Together they let us sample ancient Halley dust twice a year.

shower/perseids.description: The Perseids are the most popular meteor shower of the year, peaking on warm August nights at up to 100 meteors per hour. Debris shed by Comet Swift-Tuttle burns up high in Earth's atmosphere, producing fast, bright meteors — many leaving persistent glowing trains — radiating from the constellation Perseus.
shower/perseids.fun_fact: The parent of the Perseids, Comet Swift-Tuttle, has a nucleus 26 km wide — larger than the object thought to have caused the mass extinction that ended the dinosaurs. The comet last passed through the inner solar system in 1992 and will not return until 2125.

shower/puppidvelids.description: The Puppid-Velids are a complex of overlapping minor showers radiating from the constellations Puppis and Vela in the southern Milky Way. Peaking at around 10 meteors per hour, they are best observed from the southern hemisphere, where the radiant rises high in December skies.
shower/puppidvelids.fun_fact: The Puppid-Velids are thought to be debris from several different parent comets rather than a single source, including Comet 26P/Grigg-Skjellerup. Their southern radiant never rises above the horizon for observers at latitudes north of about 40°N, making them a shower that most of the world rarely sees.

shower/quadrantids.description: The Quadrantids are a prolific January meteor shower with a very sharp, brief peak lasting only a few hours. The radiant lies in the constellation Boötes, near the position of the defunct constellation Quadrans Muralis after which the shower is named. Up to 120 meteors per hour are visible under ideal conditions.
shower/quadrantids.fun_fact: Unlike most major showers that originate from comets, the Quadrantids' parent body is the asteroid 2003 EH1 — thought to be the dormant nucleus of a comet that burned out centuries ago. Its existence was only confirmed in 2003.

shower/ursids.description: The Ursids are a minor shower radiating from Ursa Minor, near Polaris, making them circumpolar for northern hemisphere observers — visible all night without setting. They peak around the winter solstice at about 10 meteors per hour, and the parent comet is 8P/Tuttle.
shower/ursids.fun_fact: The Ursids occasionally produce unexpected outbursts far above their typical rate. In 1945 and again in 2006, observers recorded 50 or more meteors per hour — five times the normal peak. These surges occur when Earth threads through an unusually dense ribbon of debris shed during a close approach of Comet Tuttle.

star/achernar.description: Achernar is the brightest star in Eridanus (the River) and the ninth-brightest star in the night sky.
star/achernar.fun_fact: Achernar is the flattest star known! It spins so fast that its equatorial diameter is 56% larger than its polar diameter.

star/acrux.description: Acrux (Alpha Crucis) is the brightest star in the Southern Cross and the 13th brightest star in the sky.
star/acrux.fun_fact: Acrux appears on the flags of Australia, New Zealand, Brazil, Papua New Guinea, and Samoa!

star/adhara.description: Adhara (Epsilon Canis Majoris) is the second-brightest star in Canis Major, after Sirius.
star/adhara.fun_fact: About 4.7 million years ago, Adhara was the brightest star in the night sky, even brighter than Sirius is today!

star/alcyone.description: Alcyone is the brightest star in the Pleiades cluster (M45) in the constellation Taurus. It's a blue-white giant star.
star/alcyone.fun_fact: Alcyone is actually a multiple star system with at least three companions! It also spins so fast that it has a disc of gas around its equator.

star/aldebaran.description: Aldebaran is an orange giant star that represents the eye of Taurus (the Bull). Its name means "the follower" in Arabic.
star/aldebaran.fun_fact: Aldebaran appears to be part of the Hyades star cluster but is actually only half the distance to us - a cosmic optical illusion!

star/alderamin.description: Alderamin is the brightest star in Cepheus (the King). Its name comes from Arabic meaning "the right arm."
star/alderamin.fun_fact: Due to Earth's axial precession, Alderamin will become the North Pole Star around the year 7500 AD!

star/algenib.description: Algenib marks a corner of the Great Square of Pegasus. It's a hot blue subgiant star and a Beta Cephei variable.
star/algenib.fun_fact: Algenib pulsates, changing its brightness slightly every 3.6 hours! It's also one of the most distant stars that form a prominent asterism visible to the naked eye.

star/algieba.description: Algieba is a beautiful double star in Leo (the Lion), forming the mane of the celestial lion. Its name means "the forehead" in Arabic.
star/algieba.fun_fact: Through a telescope, Algieba splits into a stunning pair of golden and yellow-orange giant stars — one of the finest double stars in the sky! A planet was discovered orbiting the primary star in 2009.

star/algol.description: Algol is a famous eclipsing binary star in Perseus, known as the "Demon Star" since ancient times.
star/algol.fun_fact: Every 2.87 days, Algol dims noticeably as its dimmer companion passes in front - ancient astronomers found this spooky!

star/alhena.description: Alhena marks the foot of Pollux, one of the twins in Gemini. It's a bright white subgiant star and one of Gemini's most prominent stars.
star/alhena.fun_fact: Alhena's name comes from Arabic meaning "the brand mark" — ancient Arabs saw this star as a brand on the neck of a camel!

star/alioth.description: Alioth is the brightest star in Ursa Major and the brightest star in the Plough asterism.
star/alioth.fun_fact: Alioth has a peculiar magnetic field that causes chemical elements to concentrate in spots on its surface!

star/alkaid.description: Alkaid is the star at the tip of the Plough's handle in Ursa Major. It's the third-brightest star in Ursa Major.
star/alkaid.fun_fact: Unlike most stars in The Plough, Alkaid is not part of the Ursa Major Moving Group — it's travelling through space in a different direction, so The Plough's shape will slowly change over thousands of years!

star/alnair.description: Alnair is the brightest star in Grus (the Crane). Its name means "the bright one" in Arabic.
star/alnair.fun_fact: Alnair spins extremely rapidly — at least 215 km/s at its equator — which is so fast that the star is noticeably oblate, bulging at its middle!

star/alnath.description: Alnath is the second-brightest star in Taurus, marking the tip of the bull's northern horn. It lies right on the Taurus-Auriga border.
star/alnath.fun_fact: Alnath was once shared between two constellations! It was designated both Beta Tauri and Gamma Aurigae before the IAU officially assigned it to Taurus in 1930.

star/alnilam.description: Alnilam is the middle star of Orion's Belt and one of the most luminous stars known in our galaxy.
star/alnilam.fun_fact: Alnilam is losing mass at a rate of 20 million times faster than our Sun through its powerful stellar wind!

star/alphard.description: Alphard is the brightest star in Hydra (the Water Snake), the largest constellation in the sky.
star/alphard.fun_fact: Alphard means "the solitary one" in Arabic because it sits alone in an otherwise dim region of sky!

star/alphekka.description: Alphekka (also called Gemma) is the brightest star in Corona Borealis (the Northern Crown). It's the jewel of this small circlet of stars.
star/alphekka.fun_fact: Alphekka is an eclipsing binary — its faint companion passes in front of it every 17.4 days, causing a tiny dip in brightness that's nearly impossible to see without instruments!

star/alpheratz.description: Alpheratz is the brightest star in Andromeda, though it was once considered part of Pegasus.
star/alpheratz.fun_fact: Alpheratz has an extremely unusual chemical composition with high concentrations of mercury and manganese in its atmosphere!

star/altair.description: Altair is the brightest star in Aquila (the Eagle) and one of the closest stars visible to the naked eye.
star/altair.fun_fact: Altair rotates so fast (once every 9 hours) that it's noticeably flattened at its poles - it's 14% wider than it is tall!

star/ankaa.description: Ankaa is the brightest star in Phoenix, a constellation best seen from the Southern Hemisphere. Its name comes from the Arabic word for "the phoenix."
star/ankaa.fun_fact: Ankaa is a spectroscopic binary star, meaning its companion is so close that the two can only be detected by shifts in their light spectrum — they orbit each other every 10.2 years!

star/antares.description: Antares is a red supergiant star, the heart of Scorpius (the Scorpion). Its name means "rival of Mars" due to its red colour.
star/antares.fun_fact: Antares is so large that if placed in our solar system, its surface would extend past the orbit of Mars!

star/arcturus.description: Arcturus is the brightest star in the northern hemisphere, an orange giant in the constellation Boötes (the Herdsman).
star/arcturus.fun_fact: Arcturus is travelling through space at a tremendous speed and will pass closest to our solar system in about 4,000 years!

star/arneb.description: Arneb is the brightest star in Lepus (the Hare), the constellation crouching beneath Orion's feet. It's a rare white supergiant.
star/arneb.fun_fact: Arneb is a dying star that has likely already fused all its core hydrogen. It may end its life as a supernova within the next few million years!

star/betelgeuse.description: Betelgeuse is a red supergiant star marking the shoulder of Orion. It's one of the largest stars visible to the naked eye.
star/betelgeuse.fun_fact: Betelgeuse is so large that if placed at our Sun's position, it would engulf Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, and possibly Jupiter!

star/canopus.description: Canopus is the second-brightest star in the night sky. It's visible mainly from the Southern Hemisphere.
star/canopus.fun_fact: Canopus is used by spacecraft for navigation because it's very bright and far from the ecliptic plane!

star/capella.description: Capella is the brightest star in Auriga and the sixth-brightest in the night sky. It's actually a system of four stars.
star/capella.fun_fact: Capella means "little goat" in Latin. Ancient cultures saw it as a goat carried on the shoulder of Auriga, the Charioteer!

star/caph.description: Caph is the second-brightest star in Cassiopeia, forming the rightmost point of the iconic W-shape. Its name means "the palm" in Arabic.
star/caph.fun_fact: Caph is a Delta Scuti variable — it pulsates with multiple frequencies simultaneously, changing brightness slightly every 2.5 hours!

star/castor.description: Castor is one of the twin stars in Gemini. Though it appears as one star, it's actually a system of six stars!
star/castor.fun_fact: Castor is a sextuple star system - three pairs of binary stars all orbiting each other. It's one of the most complex star systems near Earth!

star/deneb.description: Deneb marks the tail of Cygnus (the Swan). It's part of the Summer Triangle asterism along with Vega and Altair.
star/deneb.fun_fact: Deneb is one of the most distant stars visible to the naked eye, located about 2,600 light-years away!

star/denebola.description: Denebola marks the tail of Leo (the Lion). Its name literally means "tail of the lion" in Arabic.
star/denebola.fun_fact: Denebola has a dusty debris disc that may indicate planets are forming or asteroids are colliding around it!

star/diphda.description: Diphda (Beta Ceti) is the brightest star in Cetus (the Sea Monster) and a prominent autumn star.
star/diphda.fun_fact: Diphda appears isolated in a rather barren region of sky, making it useful for navigators despite not being extremely bright!

star/dubhe.description: Dubhe is one of the two "pointer stars" in the Plough that point to Polaris, the North Star.
star/dubhe.fun_fact: Unlike most Plough stars, Dubhe and Alkaid are moving in the opposite direction - the asterism will look different in 50,000 years!

star/e_lyrae.description: Epsilon Lyrae is a multiple star system in Lyra, famous among observers as the "Double Double".
star/e_lyrae.fun_fact: Sharp eyes can split Epsilon Lyrae into two stars - and a telescope splits each of those into two again! It holds at least five stars in total.

star/enif.description: Enif is the brightest star in Pegasus and marks the nose of the flying horse in the constellation.
star/enif.fun_fact: In 1972, Enif experienced a dramatic flare event, briefly increasing its brightness by a factor of five!

star/etamin.description: Etamin (also Eltanin) is the brightest star in Draco (the Dragon). It represents the dragon's head, and its name means "the great serpent" in Arabic.
star/etamin.fun_fact: Observations of Etamin in 1728 by James Bradley led to the discovery of the aberration of light — one of the first direct proofs that Earth moves through space!

star/fomalhaut.description: Fomalhaut is the brightest star in Piscis Austrinus and one of the brightest stars in the autumn sky.
star/fomalhaut.fun_fact: Fomalhaut has a spectacular debris disc that was one of the first to be directly imaged around another star!

star/hadar.description: Hadar (Beta Centauri) is the second-brightest star in Centaurus and the 11th brightest in the night sky.
star/hadar.fun_fact: Hadar and Alpha Centauri are known as the "Southern Pointers" - they point to the Southern Cross constellation!

star/hamal.description: Hamal is the brightest star in Aries and was once used to mark the vernal equinox about 2,000 years ago.
star/hamal.fun_fact: A giant exoplanet was discovered orbiting Hamal in 2011, at least 1.8 times Jupiter's mass!

star/izar.description: Izar is a beautiful double star in Boötes (the Herdsman). Its name means "the girdle" or "veil" in Arabic.
star/izar.fun_fact: The 19th-century astronomer Friedrich Georg Wilhelm von Struve called Izar "Pulcherrima" (Latin for "most beautiful") because of the stunning colour contrast between its orange and blue-white components!

star/j052512+062100.description: Bellatrix marks the left shoulder of Orion (the Hunter). Its name is Latin for "female warrior".
star/j052512+062100.fun_fact: Bellatrix is only about 28 million years old, and will burn through its hydrogen in another 7 million years - a brief life for a star!

star/j054048-015624.description: Alnitak is the easternmost star of Orion's Belt, sitting beside the Flame and Horsehead Nebulae.
star/j054048-015624.fun_fact: Alnitak is the brightest O-class star in the entire night sky! In about a million years it will swell wider than Jupiter's orbit and explode as a supernova.

star/j055924+445700.description: Menkalinan is the second-brightest star in Auriga (the Charioteer). Its name means "shoulder of the rein-holder" in Arabic.
star/j055924+445700.fun_fact: Menkalinan is really two nearly identical stars eclipsing each other every 47.5 hours - and in about a million years it will become the brightest star in our night sky!

star/j062248-175736.description: Mirzam (Beta Canis Majoris) rises just before Sirius, which earned it a name meaning "The Announcer" in Arabic.
star/j062248-175736.fun_fact: About four million years ago Mirzam was the brightest star in the sky, blazing at magnitude -3.65 - far brighter than Sirius appears today!

star/j070824-262324.description: Wezen is a yellow-white supergiant in Canis Major (the Greater Dog). Its name comes from the Arabic for "weight".
star/j070824-262324.fun_fact: If Wezen sat as close to us as Sirius does, it would shine as brightly as a half-full Moon!

star/j082248-593036.description: Avior (Epsilon Carinae) is a bright double star in Carina and one of the four stars of the False Cross.
star/j082248-593036.fun_fact: The False Cross is so often mistaken for the Southern Cross that it has caused real navigation errors! Avior's name was invented by British almanac makers in the 1930s.

star/j091312-694312.description: Miaplacidus is the second-brightest star in Carina (the Keel) and marks a corner of the Diamond Cross asterism.
star/j091312-694312.fun_fact: Miaplacidus has swollen into a giant after using up the hydrogen in its core, yet it still spins at a brisk 146 km/s!

star/j123112-570636.description: Gacrux (Gamma Crucis) is the topmost star of the Southern Cross and the nearest red giant star to Earth.
star/j123112-570636.fun_fact: Gacrux is the closest M-type red giant to us, and its name is simply a navigator's contraction of "Gamma Crucis" coined in the 1940s!

star/j124800-594124.description: Mimosa (Beta Crucis) is the second-brightest star in the Southern Cross and one of the hottest stars visible to the naked eye.
star/j124800-594124.fun_fact: Mimosa is a pulsating Beta Cephei variable - it swells and shrinks in three overlapping rhythms, each lasting only about four hours!

star/j143936-605024.description: Toliman (Alpha Centauri B) is the orange companion in the closest star system to the Sun, orbiting the brighter Rigil Kentaurus.
star/j143936-605024.fun_fact: Toliman got its official name only in 2018. It is slightly smaller and cooler than the Sun, and together with its two siblings makes up our nearest stellar neighbours!

star/j164836-690148.description: Atria is the brightest star of Triangulum Australe (the Southern Triangle), an orange giant far larger than the Sun.
star/j164836-690148.fun_fact: Atria is 139 times the Sun's diameter - placed at the centre of the Solar System it would nearly reach the orbit of Venus!

star/j173712-430000.description: Sargas is a bright giant in the tail of Scorpius (the Scorpion), bearing a traditional name of Sumerian origin.
star/j173712-430000.fun_fact: Sargas spins so fast that it bulges outward - it is a third wider across the equator than pole to pole, and may have formed when two stars merged!

star/j202548-564348.description: Peacock is the brightest star in Pavo (the Peacock), a hot blue-white star of the far southern sky.
star/j202548-564348.fun_fact: Peacock was named in the 1930s because the RAF insisted every star in its new Air Almanac have a name - and this one had none!

star/kaus_australis.description: Kaus Australis is the brightest star in Sagittarius (the Archer). Its name means "the southern bow" in a mix of Arabic and Latin.
star/kaus_australis.fun_fact: Kaus Australis lies near the direction of the centre of our Milky Way galaxy! When you look at this star, you're gazing toward the densest part of the galactic plane.

star/kochab.description: Kochab is the second-brightest star in Ursa Minor (the Little Bear). Together with Pherkad, it forms the "Guardians of the Pole."
star/kochab.fun_fact: Around 1500 BC, Kochab was the closest bright star to the north celestial pole, making it the "Pole Star" for ancient Egyptians and Phoenician sailors!

star/markab.description: Markab is one of the four stars forming the Great Square of Pegasus, an easily recognisable asterism.
star/markab.fun_fact: Markab is a "late B-type" star that's just finishing its main sequence life and will soon become a red giant!

star/menkar.description: Menkar is a red giant star that marks the nose of Cetus (the Sea Monster). Its name means "the nostril" in Arabic.
star/menkar.fun_fact: Menkar is nearing the end of its stellar life. This ageing red giant is fusing helium in its core and will eventually shed its outer layers to become a planetary nebula!

star/merak.description: Merak is one of the two "Pointer Stars" in the Plough that point the way to Polaris, the North Star. It lies in Ursa Major.
star/merak.fun_fact: Merak has an infrared excess that suggests it has a circumstellar debris disk — possibly a ring of dust and rocky material similar to our asteroid belt!

star/mirach.description: Mirach is a red giant star in Andromeda, often used as a guide to find the Andromeda Galaxy.
star/mirach.fun_fact: Mirach's Ghost is a small galaxy (NGC 404) that appears very close to Mirach - it was hidden by the star's glare for centuries!

star/mirphak.description: Mirphak (also Mirfak) is the brightest star in Perseus, a yellow-white supergiant at the heart of the Alpha Persei Cluster.
star/mirphak.fun_fact: Mirphak is surrounded by a beautiful open star cluster (Melotte 20) that's best seen with binoculars — a scattering of young, blue-white stars that move together through space!

star/n25.description: R Coronae Borealis is a rare yellow supergiant in Corona Borealis, and the prototype of the variable-star class named after it.
star/n25.fun_fact: R Coronae Borealis is sometimes called a "reverse nova" - instead of flaring up, it unpredictably fades by up to 9 magnitudes when it puffs out clouds of carbon soot that hide it from view!

star/nunki.description: Nunki is the second-brightest star in Sagittarius and the oldest star name still in common use.
star/nunki.fun_fact: The name Nunki comes from ancient Babylon where it represented the city of Eridu on the celestial sphere!

star/phad.description: Phad (also Phecda) is one of the stars forming the bowl of the Plough in Ursa Major. Its name means "the thigh" in Arabic.
star/phad.fun_fact: Phad is a member of the Ursa Major Moving Group — a set of stars that were born together and travel through space as a loose cluster, including most Plough stars!

star/polaris.description: Polaris, the North Star, appears nearly motionless in the sky while other stars rotate around it throughout the night.
star/polaris.fun_fact: Polaris is actually a triple star system! The main star is a supergiant about 2,500 times brighter than our Sun.

star/pollux.description: Pollux is the brighter of the twin stars in Gemini. Unlike Castor, it's a single orange giant star.
star/pollux.fun_fact: Pollux has a confirmed exoplanet! Pollux b is a gas giant at least twice as massive as Jupiter.

star/procyon.description: Procyon is a bright star in the constellation Canis Minor (the Lesser Dog). It's one of our closer stellar neighbours.
star/procyon.fun_fact: Procyon means "before the dog" in Greek because it rises just before Sirius, the Dog Star, in the night sky!

star/rasalhague.description: Rasalhague is the brightest star in Ophiuchus (the Serpent-Bearer), a constellation associated with healing.
star/rasalhague.fun_fact: Rasalhague is a rapid rotator - it spins so fast that it's noticeably flattened, completing a rotation in just 18 hours!

star/regulus.description: Regulus is the brightest star in Leo (the Lion) and represents the lion's heart. It's a multiple star system.
star/regulus.fun_fact: Regulus spins so fast it's nearly tearing itself apart! It completes a rotation in just 16 hours.

star/rigel.description: Rigel is a blue supergiant star marking the foot of Orion. Despite being farther than Betelgeuse, it appears similarly bright.
star/rigel.fun_fact: Rigel shines with the light of about 120,000 Suns! It's one of the most luminous stars in our region of the Milky Way.

star/rigil_kentaurus_a.description: Alpha Centauri is the closest star system to the Sun, consisting of three stars including Proxima Centauri.
star/rigil_kentaurus_a.fun_fact: Proxima Centauri, part of this system, has a potentially habitable planet! Proxima b is only 4.2 light-years away.

star/saiph.description: Saiph marks the lower-right knee of Orion. Despite appearing dimmer than Rigel, it's actually a very hot and luminous blue supergiant.
star/saiph.fun_fact: Saiph appears fainter than its temperature would suggest because most of its energy is radiated as ultraviolet light, invisible to our eyes! It's actually one of the hottest bright stars in the sky.

star/scheat.description: Scheat is a red giant star in the Great Square of Pegasus, notable for its deep orange-red colour.
star/scheat.fun_fact: Scheat is a semi-regular variable star, changing brightness over periods ranging from weeks to months!

star/shaula.description: Shaula is the second-brightest star in Scorpius and marks the scorpion's stinger in the tail.
star/shaula.fun_fact: Shaula means "the raised tail" in Arabic. It's actually a triple star system with the stars very close together!

star/shedir.description: Shedir (also Schedar) is the brightest star in Cassiopeia, an orange giant at the base of the famous W pattern. Its name means "the breast" in Arabic.
star/shedir.fun_fact: Shedir was once thought to be a variable star, but modern measurements show its brightness is remarkably steady — earlier reports of variability were likely due to primitive equipment!

star/sirius.description: Sirius is the brightest star in the night sky, located in the constellation Canis Major (the Greater Dog).
star/sirius.fun_fact: Sirius is actually a binary star system! Sirius B, its companion, is a white dwarf about the size of Earth but nearly as massive as the Sun.

star/spica.description: Spica is the brightest star in Virgo and one of the 20 brightest stars in the night sky. It's a binary star system.
star/spica.fun_fact: Spica is so close to the ecliptic that it can be occulted by the Moon. The name means "ear of wheat" in Latin!

star/unukalhai.description: Unukalhai is the brightest star in Serpens Caput (the Serpent's Head). Its name means "the neck of the serpent" in Arabic.
star/unukalhai.fun_fact: Serpens is the only constellation split into two separate parts — Serpens Caput (head) and Serpens Cauda (tail) — divided by Ophiuchus, and Unukalhai is the brightest star in the head half!

star/vega.description: Vega is one of the brightest stars visible from Earth, located in the constellation Lyra (the Harp).
star/vega.fun_fact: Vega was the North Star about 14,000 years ago and will be again in about 12,000 years due to Earth's wobble!

star/vindemiatrix.description: Vindemiatrix is the third-brightest star in Virgo (the Maiden). Its name means "the grape gatherer" in Latin.
star/vindemiatrix.fun_fact: Vindemiatrix got its name because its heliacal rising (first appearance at dawn) once coincided with the grape harvest season in the Mediterranean — it was the vintner's star!
